Grade 7 Science Lesson Plan: Photosynthesis

Grade: 7  |  Subject: Life Science  |  Topic: Photosynthesis
Duration: 60 minutes  |  Class size: 24–30 students
Prerequisites: Basic knowledge of plant parts (leaf, stem, root) and the idea that living things need energy.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  1. Identify the inputs (carbon dioxide, water, light energy) and outputs (glucose and oxygen) of photosynthesis.
  2. Write the word equation for photosynthesis and explain what each part represents.
  3. Describe the role of chlorophyll and chloroplasts in capturing light energy.
  4. Explain why plants are considered producers and why photosynthesis matters to nearly all food chains.
  5. Design and interpret a simple controlled observation showing that light is required for photosynthesis.

Materials

Whole class

  • Projector or whiteboard with a labelled leaf cross-section diagram
  • Word equation card (large print) for display
  • Two potted plants of similar size and health (e.g., pothos or geranium)
  • Aluminium foil (enough to fully wrap one leaf on one plant)
  • Clothes pegs or paper clips (to hold foil in place)
  • Bromothymol blue (BTB) indicator solution or a small bottle of pondweed in water (optional, for demonstration)

Per group (4 students per group, about 6–7 groups)

  • 1 small green leaf (fresh, from a class plant or school garden)
  • 1 clear jar or beaker with water and a pinch of sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda) as a CO₂ source
  • Sticky notes in two colours (inputs and outputs)
  • Student worksheet and pencil
  • Exit ticket slip (one per student)

Timed Activity Schedule

Time Segment Teacher activity Student activity
0:00–0:05
(5 min)		 Hook Hold up a potted plant and ask: "This plant weighs more than the soil it grew in. Where did the extra mass come from?" Record responses without judging. Share predictions with a partner, then with the class.
0:05–0:15
(10 min)		 Direct instruction Present the word equation: carbon dioxide + water + light energy → glucose + oxygen. Point to chloroplasts and chlorophyll on the leaf diagram. Clarify that glucose is stored or used for energy and growth. Copy the equation and label the inputs and outputs in notes.
0:15–0:20
(5 min)		 Think-pair-share Ask: "Why can't a plant grow in a dark cupboard, even with water and soil?" Circulate and listen for key ideas. Think alone for 1 minute, discuss with a partner, and note one idea.
0:20–0:38
(18 min)		 Guided investigation: light and starch (or gas production) Show the pre-prepared setup from Day 1: a leaf fully wrapped in foil on Plant A and an unwrapped leaf on Plant B, both kept in bright light for 2–3 days. (Alternative: a pondweed jar in light vs. a jar wrapped in foil in the dark, counting oxygen bubbles over 5 minutes.) Groups observe the setup and record what they see. Prompt: "What is the only difference between the two setups?" In groups, complete the worksheet: record observations, identify the variable (light), and predict the result. Use sticky notes to place inputs and outputs on a class poster.
0:38–0:46
(8 min)		 Class synthesis Lead a discussion: "Which input provided the energy? Where did the carbon come from? Where did the oxygen go?" Correct misconceptions (e.g., plants do not get their food from soil). Groups report one finding each. Revise the class poster together.
0:46–0:54
(8 min)		 Real-world connection Ask: "How does photosynthesis connect to the food you ate today and the air you are breathing?" Briefly explain the role of producers in food chains. Draw a simple food chain starting with the sun and ending with a human, labelling where photosynthesis occurs.
0:54–1:00
(6 min)		 Exit ticket Hand out the five-question exit ticket. Collect at the door or from tables. Complete the five multiple-choice questions individually, without notes.

Teacher Notes

Content background

  • Overall equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Grade 7 students need the word equation; the chemical equation is optional enrichment.
  • Where it happens: Mainly in leaf mesophyll cells, inside chloroplasts. Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green, which is why leaves look green.
  • Gas exchange: Carbon dioxide enters through stomata (tiny pores, usually on the underside of leaves). Oxygen exits the same way.
  • Common misconception: Students often believe plants get their mass from soil. Most of the mass of a plant comes from carbon dioxide in the air, which is converted into sugars and then into cellulose and other structures. Water also contributes hydrogen and oxygen to the glucose molecule.
  • Respiration contrast: Plants also respire, using oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide. Students may confuse the two processes; a simple table comparing them helps.
Safety: Do not have students taste or eat any plant material from the investigation. Wash hands after handling leaves and soil. If using BTB or baking soda, keep solutions in labelled containers and avoid eye contact. Check for plant allergies before handling.

Preparation (complete the day before)

  • Set up the foil-covered leaf demonstration on Day 1 so that results are visible by the lesson.
  • Prepare the sticky-note poster with headings: Inputs and Outputs.
  • Print one worksheet and one exit ticket per student.
  • If live results are not feasible in time, use a pre-recorded photo of a starch-test or pondweed bubble result as a substitute.

Assessment for learning

Use the hook responses and the poster to gauge prior knowledge. The exit ticket shows individual understanding; items 1 and 4 target the most common misconceptions.

Differentiation Tips

Learner need Support strategies Extension strategies
English language learners Provide a bilingual glossary (e.g., chloroplast, stomata, glucose). Use visuals for each input and output. Allow answers in drawings or short phrases. Ask students to explain the equation in their first language to a partner, then in English.
Struggling readers or students with limited prior knowledge Provide a partially completed word equation with blanks. Offer a choice of three answers for the input and output labels. Pair with a supportive peer. Ask them to explain why the foil-covered leaf looks different from the uncovered leaf.
Students with attention or processing needs Break the investigation into smaller steps on a checklist. Give a visual timer. Allow movement during the group task (e.g., a "gallery walk" to view the poster). Give a role such as "materials manager" or "data recorder" with clear responsibilities.
Advanced learners Offer the chemical equation with balancing practice as a challenge. Ask: "Why would a plant in a very low-light forest need a larger leaf surface area?" Or: "How would adding more carbon dioxide change the rate of photosynthesis?" Students may design a follow-up experiment with a variable of their choice.
Students with fine motor challenges Pre-cut foil and pre-attach pegs. Allow students to direct a partner or use adapted tools. Ask them to lead the class synthesis discussion.

Exit Ticket: Photosynthesis

Name: ______________________    Date: ____________

Choose the best answer for each question.

1. Which of the following is a product of photosynthesis?

  1. Carbon dioxide
  2. Water
  3. Glucose
  4. Chlorophyll

2. Where does most photosynthesis take place in a plant leaf?

  1. In the roots, using soil minerals
  2. In the chloroplasts of leaf cells
  3. In the stem, using stored sugar
  4. In the flower, using pollen

3. Which gas is taken in by plants during photosynthesis?

  1. Oxygen
  2. Nitrogen
  3. Carbon dioxide
  4. Hydrogen

4. A plant is kept in a completely dark cupboard for two weeks. Which statement best explains what happens to its photosynthesis?

  1. It continues at the same rate because the plant has stored soil nutrients.
  2. It stops, because light energy is needed to drive the process.
  3. It speeds up, because plants need more oxygen in the dark.
  4. It stops only if the plant has no water.

5. Why are plants called "producers" in a food chain?

  1. They eat other organisms to get energy.
  2. They make their own food using energy from sunlight.
  3. They break down dead material in the soil.
  4. They are always the largest organisms in an ecosystem.

Answer Key

Question Correct answer Explanation (for teacher use)
1 C. Glucose Glucose is a product (output). Carbon dioxide and water are inputs; chlorophyll is a pigment that captures light and is not consumed or produced as food.
2 B. In the chloroplasts of leaf cells Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy. Roots absorb water and minerals, not sugar, and stems and flowers do not carry out most photosynthesis.
3 C. Carbon dioxide Carbon dioxide enters through stomata on leaves. Oxygen is released, not taken in, during photosynthesis.
4 B. It stops, because light energy is needed to drive the process. Light energy is a required input. Without it the light-dependent reactions cannot occur, so glucose production stops. Stored soil nutrients do not provide energy for photosynthesis.
5 B. They make their own food using energy from sunlight. Producers (autotrophs) convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose, which supports all other organisms in the food chain.
